title: How Committing to the 2-Way Forward Archetype Has Worked Out for the Red Wings
parts: The Red Wings were on a roll, and then suddenly they weren’t. The calendar flipped from February to March, and the team promptly lost the first six games of the month as part of a seven-game losing streak. All seven would have been in the month of March if it weren’t for 2024 being a leap year.

Up until that point, vibes were high. Goals were being scored at a clip the team hadn’t seen since the Ken Holland era. Patrick Kane had chosen to play for the city of Detroit as an early Christmas present, Daniel Sprong was on the heater of a lifetime with 16 goals (nearly 4 above expected), and the Red Wings were holding onto the first wild card spot in the East.

After five straight losses in March, Daniel Sprong was a healthy scratch for the first time. His 16 goals were good enough for fourth on the team, but his production was off the charts averaging just 12.6 minutes per game. He went on to be scratched four more times in March and then again April 1. When pressed, then-coach Derek Lalonde stated, “I think it’s our team game…obviously both Spronger and Berggren can produce some offense but just the rhythm or lines right now.”

This, in my mind, was the beginning of the shift towards 2-way, responsible players on the NHL roster. Also on that list of goals as of February 29 was Robby Fabbri, whose 15 goals were good enough for fifth on the team. Both he and Daniel Sprong did not return to the Red Wings for the 2024-25 season. A key reason why is that Fabbri ranked in the 3rd percentile for defense and Sprong ranked in the 6th percentile. Their offense, theoretically, did not make up for the lack of defensive responsibility.
What the Red Wings prioritized in the draft

Even though this shift may have occurred at the professional level in March 2024, it started at the prospect level almost as soon as Steve Yzerman’s tenure began. Moritz Seider was infamously taken with the 6th pick in the 2019 draft. Most draft boards didn’t even have him in the top 10, but he graded out as a potentially elite defensive defenseman. He has reached, if not surpassed that defensive potential, but his offense is where his value post-draft has skyrocketed him into superstar status.

Lucas Raymond was the Red Wings’ top pick in 2020, and no one was raving about his defensive prowess. However, the value on the table by picking him 4th was too good to pass up. Since he has been in the system, molding him into a defensively responsible forward has paid significant dividends. Despite his smaller frame, he has proven that he can keep possession in the offensive zone and get to pucks in the difficult areas. He and Mo are mirrors of each other, one great at defense who unlocked good offense, and one with great offense who unlocked passable defense.

2021 may be the last year of trying to get foundational players. With the 6th pick, they selected the perfect complementary piece to Mo Seider. Simon Edvinsson is a big, physical left-shot defenseman who has significant offensive upside. Up until now, Mo has proven to be a bit better on the offensive end, but on draft day Ed was considered the higher offensive ceiling defenseman. In theory, this tandem would be the top defensive pair for a contender. The Wings picked twice in the first round and chose Sebastian Cossa, who they believed would be the Andrei Vasilevskiy-style goalie to build around.

2022 was the year that the 2-way forward archetype went into full effect. Coming out of the draft in which they selected Marco Kasper 8th overall to be a future top 6 center, Kris Draper exclaimed, “The intensity he plays with, his compete and work ethic is off the charts.” The term “compete” would become a common thread across most top draft picks moving forward. On the professional level, the Red Wings would sign Andrew Copp to be a middle 6 center.

2023 saw Nate Danielson, another center, selected with the 9th pick of the draft. Steve Yzerman noted, “He’s a good skater, he’s got good skills and is a good two-way centerman.” Draper added, “The character and passion he has for the game, a real smart hockey player. He understands how to play in all three zones.” This was also the year the Red Wings added J.T. Compher to be another two-way center.

In 2024, so many journalists and podcasters had the pick mailed in weeks if not months before the draft. It seemed like everyone mocked Michael Brandsegg-Nygård to the Red Wings at 15, and that’s exactly what happened. “Really good two way player”, “when he’s not scoring he’ll still be an effective player”, and “competitive hockey player that can obviously think the game” were all descriptions ascribed to MBN.

And to round things out, in 2025 the Red Wings selected Carter Bear 13th overall. This one was celebrated by most fans noting that he has significant offensive upside and only fell in the draft because of a partially torn achilles. However, it should still be noted that Yzerman described him as “a very intelligent hockey player, extremely competitive,” while Draper added that “you walk out of the rink and just really appreciate the effort.”
How this translated to the professional level

The story of the 2025-26 Detroit Red Wings can sum up what fruit the March 2024 shift has borne - even strength scoring (5v5). In 2023-24, the Red Wings ranked 6th in 5v5 goals. In fact, that year they led the entire NHL in goals scored above expected with a +33 goals - xG. That number cratered the year after, falling to 29th and a -21 goals - xG. In 2025-26? How about 29th in goals - xG?

What was true about both Daniel Sprong and Robby Fabbri is that they both significantly outperformed their expected goals. Despite their warts, they were good finishers. The players the Red Wings are hoping will be their middle 6 centers - Andrew Copp and Marco Kasper - led the Red Wings last year in goals below expected. In fact, Andrew Copp was among the five worst in the entire NHL in goals below expected. He scored 9 goals with a 19.8 xG. If Andrew Copp ever scored 19 or 20 goals in a season, there would be much rejoicing in Motown.

The Red Wings expected goals at 5v5 was 146 in 2024, 163.9 in 2025 and 161.1 in 2026. That translated into 179 goals, 143 goals, and 142 goals respectively. Chances didn’t go away, but above average finishing did. But that was always a potential outcome, if not a foregone conclusion. The hypothesis the Red Wings were operating under was that the improvement in defense would outweigh the dropoff in offense. It was also stated directly by Yzerman in 2021, “Once you are a solid defensive hockey team, you’re going to be competitive. You can win a lot of nights. Over time you can add to the offense.”

So how were the Red Wings defensively? And how have they added offense? Let’s start with the offense. Alex DeBrincat was easily the most impactful offensive addition the Red Wings landed (or maybe gifted). After a down year by his standards scoring 27 goals, he has put up 39 and then 41 goals in the most recent two seasons. Patrick Kane followed Alex DeBrincat to Detroit and also put up a bunch of strong offensive numbers. He was also the exception to the shift to 2-way forwards, ranking in the 4th percentile in defense over the period of time he’s been in Detroit.

Aside from those two players, it’s bleak. From 2024 to 2025, the Red Wings have signed Vladimir Tarasenko, Christian Fischer, Tyler Motte, James van Riemsdyk, and Mason Appleton. Not stellar in terms of adding enough offense. It’s hard to imagine how dire the situation would be if Alex DeBrincat was not on this team. It’s fair to say that offense has not been as easy to add as expected.

So let’s look at defense. It is true that teams that fit the low 5v5 goal scoring but have defensively responsible forwards can still make the playoffs at a decent clip. When you have above average defense and above average goaltending, that group made the playoffs 11 out of 13 times. When you switch that to middle-middle, only 5 of 22 teams made the playoffs. In the last two years, the Red Wings ranked 22nd and 15th in chances allowed, something that should be extremely low if the forward group was as defensively responsible as they had been molding their roster to be. The goaltending was 9th and 18th respectively. That top 10 finish in goaltending was not enough to overcome the below average defense and poor offense.

The output has not been what was expected nor designed to be. The Red Wings are operating with very little margin for error on the defensive and goaltending sides, and neither has been able to hold up over the course of a season. The philosophy may not be wrong, but the roster construction definitely has missed the mark. The players they’ve handpicked to be elite 200-foot forwards have yet to turn the team into an above average defense. If what has transpired this offseason was erased, and you started getting more meaningful minutes from players like Nate Danielson, Michael Brandsegg-Nygard and Carter Mazur, and fewer minutes from the guys labeled “jerseys”, we may finally see a playoff team. Sadly, the 5-3 victory over the Ottawa Senators on October 6 may have just been a glimpse to the type of team we could have been.
What teams who prioritized 2-way forwards were most successful?

If you’re going to mold your team into this type of hard-to-play-against roster, the logical question is, “Who showed that was possible?” The easy answer is Carolina, but they just won the Stanley Cup, which comes long after this roster reconstruction and drafting philosophy began. There’s a few filters we need to put on to get to the likely models for this current iteration of the Red Wings, how close they are, and whether or not ultimate success could have been achieved on their current path.

First, we have to look at teams that won prior to 2021 but still recent enough that they could be considered a modern roster construction. Second, they need to be teams whose forwards were above average to elite on the defensive end. Third, we’re looking at teams that may not have relied heavily on 5v5 scoring, which tends to be a byproduct of more defensive-minded teams. And lastly, they most likely can’t have a star player who is superstar Connor McDavid or Nathan MacKinnon level. Remember: Dylan Larkin is the star player we are building this around as our 1C.

The team that jumps off the page immediately is the 2011-2014 Los Angeles Kings who won 2 cups in three years. Their star player was Anze Kopitar, who ranked 16th in scoring in their first cup season, but was backed up by Jonathan Quick who had a monster year ranking 2nd in goals saved above expected. They ranked 29th in 5v5 scoring during their first cup run, and only 25th in their second cup run. However, in both seasons they had top 5 forward defense and top 3 goaltending. Drew Doughty was their top defenseman.

If Sebastian Cossa would have progressed as expected, I believe the Red Wings felt they could have similar elite goaltending, albeit not necessarily as elite as Quick was in those two seasons. Mo Seider is better than Drew Doughty was during the Kings mini dynasty, too. Seider comes out ahead in goals above replacement by a significant margin (especially over the last two years) while also having more extreme expected goals share (xG share) splits. The Kings still hovered between 52-55% xG share when Doughty was off the ice. The Red Wings were at 55% with Seider on, and 46% with him off.

This leaves us with the known commodities: Dylan Larkin vs. Anze Kopitar. The one thing Larkin has going for him that Kopitar never really excelled at during this period is goal scoring. Larkin has averaged 76 points per 82 over the last two seasons, which is in the same ballpark (or arena) as Kopitar’s 73. Larkin’s 36 goals per 82 are significantly more than Kopitar’s 24. But that’s where stats that favor Larkin end. And actually, when adjusted for era, Kopitar’s points per 82 actually ranked in the 16th to 28th range while Larkin’s ranked between 41st to 50th.

The true difference between Kopitar and Larkin happens at the defensive end. The star player for the Kings was also the prototype of the type of roster they wanted to create. No one was a better defensive forward than Kopitar on his team. He ranked on average in the 83rd percentile for even-strength defense among forwards while also ranking in the 76th percentile for even-strength offense. The even strength expected goals share was an average of 60% with him on the ice and 52% with him off. If you were to sum it up, Kopitar at his peak was a top-10 forward who drove play across all 200 feet of the ice - a true 2-way forward.

Larkin in those same metrics is fairly average. He has ranked in the 67th percentile in even-strength offense over the last three seasons, while being below average on defense (38th percentile). He also did not move the needle in 5v5 xG share. The Red Wings averaged a 48% xG share with him on the ice and a 47% xG share with him off the ice. Larkin is a decent goal scorer for a 1C whose line is consistently unable to tilt the ice. This murkiness in terms of the type of player Dylan Larkin is compared to the type of team the Red Wings are trying to construct may actually be an inhibitor to success. Larkin’s main value actually comes from being good enough as a 1C that allows the lack of depth at center on the Red Wings to not be easily exploited.

The team that may be most similar to the Red Wings that won the Stanley Cup is the 2018-19 St. Louis Blues. Led by Ryan O’Reilly and Alex Pietrangelo, the Blues were an unlikely winner. They ranked 3rd in forward defense, but just 17th in goaltending and 16th in scoring. However, the Red Wings still lack a 2-way forward at the level of the Selke-winning O’Reilly. It’s hard to project the Red Wings current roster into any of the cup-winning teams they may have been modeled against.
The peak for this iteration of the Detroit Red Wings

Okay, so if winning the Stanley Cup is not the trajectory this team could have been on, what is the actual ceiling? And I’m not talking for this year. This is based on if everything goes right and they fill out their roster with realistic moves that can make them better around the margins. I used a distance metric where the lower the coefficient, the more similar they are. Number three on that list is actually the 2011-12 cup-winning Kings, but for the reasons laid out above, that’s not really that realistic. There are two teams with a tiny gap between each other and a large gap from 2nd to the 3rd place Kings team. I’m talking about the 2016-17 Tampa Bay Lightning and the 2019-20 New York Islanders.

It may come as no surprise that the roster the Red Wings are most similar to is the one Steve Yzerman also had his fingerprints all over. That team was middle of the pack on defense and goaltending, but had an elite defenseman in Victor Hedman. Nikita Kucherov was also 6th in scoring that year, so you might pencil in Alex DeBrincat as the comp for that season. What happened? They missed the playoffs. What happened after that? Kucherov went off the charts, Hedman continued to be elite, and Andrei Vasilevskiy became the best goalie in the world. Aside from Seider being a great comp to Hedman in terms of difference-making, no one else on this Red Wings roster projects to become what that Lightning team became.

The comp that I think makes the most sense is the 2019-20 New York Islanders. They did not have a top scoring center. Mathew Barzal ranked 29th that year. They did have an elite defenseman in Ryan Pulock who ranked 2nd in Evolving Hockey’s goals above replacement (Seider ranked 2nd last year as well). And finally, they had average goaltending. The rest of their forward group propelled them to a 10th place finish in defense, which is not out of the question for a Red Wings team who ranked 15th last year. If the young players on the Red Wings are able to step up and provide an improvement in forward defense, that number is even likely. That Islanders team lost in the Conference Finals.

So what does all this mean? Although it is highly unlikely that this Red Wings core would have reached or even won the Stanley Cup, they were most likely on a trajectory to achieve moderate playoff success. At the very least, they would have ended the longest current playoff drought in the NHL. As it stands, if Larkin truly does end up leaving for futures, we’ll never know what would have been.
